title: Initial biochemical assessment of hypercalcemia
fairness: Repeat calcium, albumin and intact PTH is the best offered initial investigation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The stone does not create a second consequential inference: the answer follows from an isolated elevated calcium without a PTH result. PTHrP and urinary clearance are downstream branches, so this remains basic first-test recall.

First node is coherent and self-contained; its explanation does not disclose R02's operative answer. This is a high-yield diagnostic sequence, but the present task does not meet the resident reasoning target.

All entries are offline editorial reviews of candidate visible fields and preceding candidate feedback, not source re-verification or clinical approval. Runtime rendering and wait estimates cannot be established from these fields.
suggestions: Introduce a meaningful conflict in the prior calcium/PTH record or a decision-relevant sampling issue, then compare plausible next biochemical assessments. Do not add extra laboratory values unless their interpretation changes the choice.

title: Stone-associated PHPT despite a reference-range PTH
clarityIssues: 'Have not supported an inherited calcium disorder' summarizes a completed workup rather than showing its result; understandable here because inherited-disorder testing is not the scored decision.
fairness: Parathyroidectomy assessment is the single best offered pathway: recognize that a reference-range PTH is inappropriate during hypercalcemia, then apply documented recurrent stone disease.
The two competing nonsurgical pathways are less appropriate as the recommendation at this stage; no refusal or operative contraindication is supplied. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The four-week update follows R01 coherently, supplies the needed results, and supports the task without relying on a previously correct answer. R01 feedback does not give away the operative indication.

title: Completing skeletal assessment in PHPT
clarityIssues: 'Which additional skeletal investigation' does not specify whether the decision is completion of density-site acquisition or assessment for occult vertebral fracture.
The exhibit identifies two acquired DXA sites but does not establish whether vertebral fracture assessment has already been done.
fairness: Distal one-third-radius DXA completes the missing density site, but vertebral fracture assessment is also a defensible additional component of PHPT skeletal evaluation. Absence of reported fractures does not establish absence of occult vertebral fractures.

The explanation ranks VFA by a narrower goal, 'complete the absent recommended forearm density acquisition,' that the task never states. The options cannot be uniquely ranked under the broad task as written.

Even after narrowing the task, identifying the omitted third site is one rule, not two consequential clinical steps. This is high-yield content, but should not be made difficult through an ambiguous goal.
suggestions: Resolve the competing VFA indication explicitly. Either ask a clearly scoped density-acquisition question and acknowledge its basic difficulty, or supply an actual acquisition/interpretation problem with a consequential next decision.
Do not simply delete VFA and replace it with an implausible investigation; build competing plans that address the same defined objective.

title: Age-based operative assessment in biochemically established PHPT
fairness: The best offered pathway is parathyroidectomy assessment: infer PTH-dependent hypercalcemia despite a PTH within range, then recognize the independent age criterion despite reassuring organ assessment.

The normal renal and skeletal findings are decision-relevant competitors rather than gratuitous exclusions. Surveillance is a real alternative if surgery is not selected, but does not negate recommending operative assessment.
The standalone record supplies repeat testing, mimic evaluation and the relevant age. No confident clinical inaccuracy or material wording shortcut identified.

title: Urinary calcium evaluation of familial hypercalcemia

cues.why: Together with the completed serum pattern, this makes 'Repeat serum calcium, albumin and intact PTH' a conspicuously redundant option. The key is the only offered investigation that adds the missing type of measurement.

fairness: Concurrent serum and 24-hour urinary calcium/creatinine is the best offered biochemical investigation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Family history points directly to the familiar FHH workup; repeat serum studies and PTHrP provide little competition after the nonsuppressed-PTH pattern is given. Recognize-a-pattern then recall-its-test does not create two consequential steps here.
R05 is a coherent first node and its feedback does not explicitly supply R06's genetic-panel answer.
suggestions: Make collection adequacy, a real confound, or a discordant family result change the next biochemical action. Compare credible tests or preparation strategies at that same stage.
Retain enough medication, renal and vitamin D information to make the selected interpretation fair; do not manufacture difficulty by withholding it.

title: Genetic clarification after low calcium clearance and familial disease
fairness: Genetic evaluation is the best offered next investigation after an interpretable low clearance ratio plus multiple affected relatives. The explanation appropriately avoids treating the ratio as independently diagnostic.

Interpret the ratio in the family/medication/renal context, then choose diagnostic clarification rather than localization for an assumed operation. Repeating an adequate collection is the closest plausible sequencing error.

R05 feedback scaffolds the purpose of the collection but does not state the genetic-panel answer. The current update and retained presentation give the needed data without requiring the earlier answer.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this editorial PASS does not establish the completeness or yield of a particular genetic assay.

title: Thiazide exposure during urinary calcium testing
clarityIssues: 'Review thiazide therapy' does not specify what changes before recollection; merely reviewing the medication could leave the confound unchanged.
'Replace cholecalciferol' is ambiguous between replenishing vitamin D and substituting another drug; no cholecalciferol use is described.

cues.why: The only named exposure maps directly to the only option saying 'thiazide therapy'; the other modifying option targets a measurement already stated to be normal.
This explicitly undercuts the cholecalciferol distractor, leaving a medication-review versus unchanged-medications choice.

fairness: Thiazide exposure is a valid reason to reconsider interpretation of a low clearance ratio. The keyed direction is reasonable, but its action is less concrete than the explanation and later node assume.
The ratio's actual value adds little to choosing the uniquely named confound-removal pathway. The task is easy despite a clinically important principle.
N02 assumes supervised withdrawal has occurred, whereas N01's chosen action only promises review. Make that transition explicit rather than implying that review equals withdrawal.
suggestions: Name the clinician-supervised preparation change precisely without inventing a washout interval.
Use credible alternative strategies requiring interpretation of the actual collection and medication record; avoid eliminating a distractor solely with a normal vitamin D sentence.

title: Persistent familial pattern after a negative genetic panel
fairness: Serial calcium review and first-degree-relative testing is the best offered investigation. A negative panel does not, by itself, establish sporadic PHPT or justify localization.

The resident must interpret residual diagnostic uncertainty after the confound is removed and genetic testing is negative, then choose a family/longitudinal investigation. Localization is a credible consequential error; PTHrP is a weaker distractor.

The update explicitly establishes thiazide withdrawal, repeat collection and the negative panel. It remains answerable with the case presentation even if N01 was missed; N01 feedback does not supply this answer.
Existing mother/uncle records are relevant evidence, not proof that every useful first-degree relative has already been tested. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Secondary drivers of normocalcemic PTH elevation

cues.phrase: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is below the laboratory range, and her diet contains little calcium
cues.why: The key uniquely repairs both explicitly named deficiencies. The two alternatives address neither and are more aggressive than correcting the supplied abnormalities.

cues.phrase: Restore calcium intake and replace cholecalciferol
cues.why: The key is the only combined corrective plan, whereas the other options are single interventions.

fairness: Correction of calcium intake and vitamin D is the best offered step before assigning normocalcemic PHPT. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This is a direct deficiency-to-replacement match rather than two consequential inferences. Cinacalcet in a normocalcemic record is particularly weak competition.
The first node and its later follow-up are chronologically coherent; the later ionized-calcium result is not exposed here.
suggestions: Build a real interpretation/management conflict around treatment response or an adequately characterized residual abnormality, with comparable specific plans.
Use 'supplement vitamin D with cholecalciferol' or similarly clear replacement wording. Do not add a second unrelated disease solely to raise difficulty.

title: Elevated ionized calcium despite normal total calcium
fairness: Hypercalcemic PHPT is the best offered biochemical classification: repeated elevated ionized calcium with elevated PTH is incompatible with the normocalcemic label, after the described reassessment.

The total-versus-ionized distinction is high-yield and a plausible resident trap. However, the task ends at classification; interpreting multiple measurements and selecting their diagnosis is still one scored inference.

N03's feedback explains correction of secondary drivers, but does not give away the later ionized-calcium result. The update clearly changes the earlier normal-calcium state and is necessary to the answer.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. A longer catalogue of exclusions should not be added merely to create apparent complexity.
suggestions: Have the interpreted ionized/total calcium discrepancy change a concrete next assessment or treatment decision, with plausible competing actions and all necessary criteria.
Keep the repeated ionized results and clear interval correction; do not replace them with the diagnostic label.

title: Operative relevance of isolated radial osteoporosis in PHPT
fairness: Parathyroidectomy assessment is the best offered pathway. The postmenopausal patient's radial T-score identifies skeletal involvement despite reassuring axial sites and relatively modest calcium elevation.
Interpret site-specific bone density, then apply its operative consequence; surveillance based on the axial sites is a credible competing error.

The comparison does not require averaging DXA sites or treating the normal hip/spine as a veto. The table is necessary to the decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy or unfair wording shortcut identified.

title: Silent renal calculus as a PHPT operative indication
clarityIssues: 'Three-site bone density is above operative thresholds' is an authored eligibility conclusion rather than actual skeletal findings; 'above' is also awkward when the relevant low-density result is expressed as a negative T-score.
fairness: Parathyroidectomy assessment is the best offered recommendation for imaging-documented nephrolithiasis in confirmed PHPT, even without colic. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The update directly supplies the single qualifying finding. The task is one-rule application: silent stone still counts. Neither cinacalcet nor surveillance presents a developed patient-specific competing consideration.
The short standalone update is coherent and necessary, but it does not create two consequential reasoning steps.
suggestions: Replace the interpreted bone-threshold statement with concise observations or remove irrelevant skeletal detail.

Use a genuine uncertainty in the renal finding or a competing patient-specific management constraint that changes the next action, with evidence sufficient to resolve it; otherwise retain only with an explicitly accepted basic teaching role.

title: Operative indication despite nonlocalizing imaging
fairness: Endocrine-surgery referral is the best offered pathway. The resident must separate a localization failure from established disease and then preserve the fracture-associated surgical indication.

The fracture and negative localization create a meaningful conflict; deleting the imaging would remove the misconception being tested. Cinacalcet and surveillance represent plausible substitution errors.
The task is clear and the referral destination is specific. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. N07 feedback supports pursuing surgery but does not prescribe N08's bilateral strategy.

title: Discordant localization and operative strategy

cues.phrase: Ultrasound identifies a left-inferior extrathyroidal candidate; sestamibi SPECT/CT identifies a right-superior focus
cues.why: The options mirror the two conflicting sides, while the key is the only plan that encompasses both. A reader can choose the inclusive option without knowing parathyroid surgical planning.
This and 'Focused right-superior parathyroidectomy' are symmetric foils; no supplied observation privileges either, making 'Bilateral parathyroid exploration' structurally dominant.

fairness: Bilateral exploration is a defensible best strategy for the supplied discordance. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Do not infer that all focused approaches are universally inappropriate: approach can depend on additional localization, intraoperative PTH and surgeon strategy. The offered side-only plans omit those features, making them weak competitors.

N07 to N08 is coherent: repeat studies identify competing candidates after initially nonlocalizing studies. N07 does not disclose the exact key, but the new option structure still makes the task easy.
suggestions: Compare complete credible operative strategies with stated use of localization and intraoperative assessment, rather than unsupported left versus right guesses.
Preserve the observed discordance; make its interpretation alter a real operative plan without using the only comprehensive option as a shortcut.

title: Hungry-bone physiology versus postoperative PTH deficiency
clarityIssues: The postoperative time course and ongoing replacement are only described qualitatively. The learner can rank mechanisms, but cannot infer a specific persistence category from this record.
'PTH within range' is described in the explanation as 'preserved PTH'; a laboratory-range result during hypocalcemia is not necessarily an appropriate physiologic response.

cues.why: This directly removes the only magnesium-based choice, leaving a two-way mechanism comparison. It is useful safety data, but the option set does not make productive use of it.

fairness: The high-turnover preoperative record plus low phosphate favors skeletal mineral uptake as the best offered explanation.

Do not teach that reference-range PTH excludes postoperative PTH insufficiency during hypocalcemia. The low phosphate and skeletal context, rather than normal-range PTH alone, are the stronger discriminator. Mixed contributions remain possible; the record does not prove they are absent.
This is a single mechanism-classification task. It may require moderate interpretation, but a mechanism and its synonymous label are not two consequential steps.
The historical hospital review is coherent with current comfort on treatment. No acute untreated emergency is implied.
suggestions: Revise the explanation to acknowledge that PTH must be interpreted relative to calcium; do not use 'preserved' as proof against PTH deficiency.

Supply the relevant observed trend and ask for a concrete replacement/monitoring decision if a two-step item is intended. Avoid invented duration cutoffs and keep acute electrolyte management within its assigned scope.

title: Activated vitamin D for postsurgical hypoparathyroidism

cues.phrase: Magnesium, kidney function and 25-hydroxyvitamin D within range
cues.why: Two of the three choices target measurements explicitly stated to be normal. The learner can remove 'Increase cholecalciferol' and 'Add magnesium chloride' without interpreting the PTH/phosphate pattern.

fairness: Adding calcitriol is the best offered medication change for the described persistent low-PTH hypocalcemic state. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The biochemical interpretation and active-vitamin-D rationale could support two-step reasoning, but the actual distractors allow the PTH and phosphate data to be bypassed.
The 14-month interval is clear, and the outpatient replacement review is coherent. Exact urgency or dosing cannot be inferred from 'below range'; neither is asked.
suggestions: Retain magnesium and vitamin D results needed for fairness, but replace the explicitly excluded supplement choices with credible calcium/active-vitamin-D management alternatives.
Make the PTH/phosphate interpretation or an observed treatment response necessary to distinguish those alternatives; do not manufacture a dose threshold.

title: Elevated PTH with normocalcemia after parathyroidectomy

cues.phrase: 25-hydroxyvitamin D was below range and dietary calcium was substantially restricted
cues.why: The key repeats both deficits as their repairs, whereas the two alternatives escalate parathyroid treatment.

cues.phrase: Replace cholecalciferol, restore intake and monitor calcium
cues.why: The key is the uniquely comprehensive three-component plan and directly matches the update.

fairness: Correcting the identified secondary drivers with calcium monitoring is the best offered plan; isolated elevated PTH with normal calcium does not establish recurrent hypercalcemic PHPT.
The prior-operation context is clinically useful, but the supplied deficiency-to-replacement match defeats the intended reasoning challenge.

The earlier nine-month stage is clearly identified and does not conflict with N12's later abnormal result. However, the explanation explicitly states that localization is premature without biochemical confirmation, rehearsing N12's subsequent key.
suggestions: Replace the direct deficit-repair shortcut with a genuine response or competing interpretation that changes the plan.
Keep adequate feedback for this node, but redesign N12 to test a distinct remaining decision rather than removing necessary teaching solely to hide the next answer.

title: Renewed hypercalcemia before reoperative localization

cues.why: This exact list makes the missing PTH conspicuous; the only option that adds it is the repeat biochemical panel.

cues.phrase: Localization and reoperative planning are premature when recurrent PHPT has not been biochemically established.
cues.why: This preceding N11 explanation states the rule that directly selects this node's laboratory-confirmation answer over 4D CT. It is prior visible feedback, not leakage from N12's own explanation.

fairness: Repeat calcium, albumin and intact PTH is the best offered investigation before assuming recurrent PHPT from a new calcium elevation and incidental focus.
The prior documented normocalcemic interval makes inherited lifelong hypercalcemia a weak alternative, so the panel distractor contributes little.

The later chronology is coherent and the task is answerable from the retained presentation/update. Independence of difficulty fails: preceding feedback already teaches the scored decision, and the item largely repeats R01's first-test rule.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; suspected recurrence is appropriately distinguished from confirmed recurrence.
suggestions: After biochemical confirmation, test a distinct reoperative decision using meaningful discordant or incomplete prior data and credible same-stage investigations.

If retaining biochemical confirmation as the objective, change the preceding sequence or coverage arrangement and add a real interpretive problem; do not claim independent two-step difficulty from an incidental scan foil.

title: Native versus active vitamin D in nondialysis CKD
fairness: Cholecalciferol is the best offered recommendation for vitamin D depletion with modest PTH elevation in the stated nondialysis setting.

The resident must interpret the renal stage and degree of PTH abnormality, then distinguish correction of a modifiable driver from reflex use of active vitamin D or a calcimimetic. Calcitriol is a credible competing renal-treatment error.
The explanation appropriately limits routine active-vitamin-D use rather than claiming it is never used in CKD. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The historical nondialysis stage is explicit. N14 supplies a later dialysis state, so the pair does not require treating those stages as simultaneous. The later operative answer is not disclosed here.

title: Refractory renal hyperparathyroidism with dose-limiting toxicity
clarityIssues: 'Persistently in a markedly elevated band' is vague for the severity assessment. The recorded symptoms and dose responses support concern, but a meaningful documented trajectory would be clearer without inventing a surgical cutoff.

cues.phrase: Higher cinacalcet doses produced symptomatic hypocalcemia; higher calcitriol doses raised phosphate despite documented binder use.
cues.why: The update explicitly says both offered dose escalations have already caused trouble. With referral as the only alternative, a reader can select it without interpreting the renal hyperparathyroidism.

fairness: Parathyroidectomy assessment is a reasonable best offered step for medically refractory severe renal hyperparathyroidism with treatment-limiting adverse effects.
The adverse effects are clinically necessary; the problem is the two unmodified escalation foils, not the inclusion of those observations. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
N13's earlier CKD visit and the later dialysis record are coherently separated. The update does all of the exclusion work, so this is not a hard two-step decision despite the longer story.
suggestions: Use credible alternative management plans that respond to the actual toxicity rather than simply repeating the failed escalations.

Provide a concise observed disease/control trajectory sufficient to judge refractoriness; do not introduce an unsupported numerical threshold or force a renal operative-extent question beyond the evidence.

title: Medical calcium lowering when PHPT surgery is not undertaken
fairness: Cinacalcet is the best offered calcium-lowering medicine. Alendronate's skeletal role and cholecalciferol's deficiency role do not make them equivalent answers to this task.

The diagnosis, nonsurgical pathway and treatment target are all supplied; the only remaining step is recalling which drug lowers calcium. This is high-yield pharmacology but not two-step resident reasoning.

Stable clinical status and operative-risk assessment are appropriate context, not inherently unfair permission cues. The degree of hypercalcemia is unspecified, so the item establishes drug choice better than it establishes a need to start treatment at that moment.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Add a consequential distinction between calcium control and another genuine treatment target using a response or competing finding, then compare credible plans.

If the task is intended to determine whether to start medication, supply the patient-specific reason for treatment. Otherwise explicitly frame medication selection after that decision, and seek acceptance as basic practice rather than claiming difficulty.

title: Separate skeletal treatment from biochemical control in PHPT

cues.why: This is the only option directed at a new target. The other two are opposite changes to cinacalcet, even though the stem already states successful calcium control.
Together with 'Withdraw cinacalcet', this produces two weak modifications of a working regimen rather than credible competing ways to address the new bone result.

fairness: Adding alendronate is the best offered response to the untreated osteoporotic skeletal target while calcium is controlled. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The intended two-step reasoning is sound: interpret the low hip density despite biochemical response, then select therapy with the appropriate target.
The current choices weaken that reasoning through a unique new-drug option and poorly motivated cinacalcet changes. The skeletal result is needed, but the comparator plans need repair.
The standalone chronology is clear. Operative risk explains the nonsurgical pathway without supplying the bone-directed drug name.
suggestions: Retain the distinct calcium and bone targets, but replace the unsupported increase/withdrawal foils with clinically credible plans at the same stage.
Include only patient-specific eligibility facts needed to distinguish the chosen bone treatment; do not add blanket assurances or invent contraindications.

title: Miami intraoperative PTH criterion and operative endpoint
clarityIssues: 'Otherwise localized single-gland PHPT case' reads as an established gland-count diagnosis; before exploration is concluded, 'localized candidate gland' would better distinguish localization from proof of single-gland disease.

cues.phrase: no second abnormal gland was seen
cues.why: This explicitly undermines 'Resect another ipsilateral parathyroid gland', making the third choice an unjustified removal rather than a credible response to an inadequate ioPTH decline.

fairness: The keyed endpoint is correct under the named conventional Miami criterion: 80 is less than half of the higher baseline, 180; its remaining above the laboratory interval does not itself invalidate the criterion.
Selecting the correct baseline, calculating the decline and applying the operative consequence are substantive steps. This is high-yield surgical reasoning, not a statistics-style exercise.
Extending exploration is a credible error if the wrong baseline or a normalization requirement is used. Blindly resecting an unspecified additional gland is not a similarly credible alternative.
No independent rule conflict is alleged here. A named standard criterion can be tested as board knowledge; any local modification would need to be stated.
suggestions: Replace the arbitrary second-gland-resection option with a credible next sampling or exploration plan, with timing and criteria made explicit and supported.
Describe preoperative localization without asserting that single-gland disease is already proven. Preserve the competing baselines and above-reference final value, which create the useful challenge.

title: Invasive parathyroid mass and oncologic resection

cues.phrase: could not be separated from the adjacent ipsilateral thyroid tissue
cues.why: This overlaps the thyroid component of the key, but it is necessary anatomic evidence for operative extent, not an unfair extraneous hint. Retain it; the learner must interpret invasive behavior rather than match a diagnosis label.

fairness: En bloc parathyroidectomy with ipsilateral thyroid lobectomy is the best offered strategy for the suspected locally invasive parathyroid malignancy.
The resident must infer oncologic concern from operative behavior, then choose an intact resection strategy rather than capsular dissection or an operation for multigland hyperplasia.

The explanation correctly treats malignancy as suspected rather than histologically proved. Actual resection extent depends on the involved structures; the option should not be read as a complete operative prescription for every possible extension.
The stopped outside exploration and later specialist review are coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; invasion and operative strategy are high-yield endocrine-surgery content.
